full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ve just got questions this time about how the placement’s going and what you’re doing and how you think it relates to your course and things like that. So, did you say you started in August?

Subject:	August the 31st, so –

Interviewer:	Been here quite a while now.

Subject:	Yeah, just over six months, I think.

Interviewer:	Okay, can you tell me a bit about the organisation that you’re working for?

Subject:	It’s called [company] and they design and manufacture all the – or a lot of the make displays they’ve got out in the shops at the moment, so all [company] stands and things like that. They also do all of the cigarette stands but that’s a different site. I'm mainly working on cosmetics.

Interviewer:	Okay, that sounds interesting. How useful do you think that your course has been so far to the work that you’re doing?

Subject:	Um, it’s a bit difficult. Some – some aspects of my course have been really helpful, but a lot of it is just learning how to use the packages and learning the way of work, which maybe I could have done without doing any of my degree at all really. I might have been slower though.

Interviewer:	Okay, what about the less technical parts of your degree, like communication skills and things like that? Do you think anything like that has helped?

Subject:	I think all the presentations we’ve done and just generally communicating an idea through drawing has been very helpful and it’s used all the time, and also the fact that on my course, because there are so many different modules, you’ve always got lots of different things going on, whereas on other courses it’s just, say, one essay to concentrate on and in my job I usually have quite a few different things going on, so I probably find it easier to keep my – to get my head around everything and remember everything.

Interviewer:	So you’ve got good time management skills?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay, is there anything in particular that you wish you had learnt before you started your placement?

Subject:	Um, not really. I mean maybe learning extra computer packages would have been helpful, but I think that whichever job you go into you can’t prepare for everything.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so maybe computers and different packages. (Yeah) Okay, do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for the placement then? (Um) Or is it the same problem again with people doing so many different things?

Subject:	I don’t think it – I don’t think there really has been a problem with my placement. I don’t think I was under-prepared for it. I think in the job, like the main aspect they are looking for somebody who’s enthusiastic and who’s hard-working and organised, which they try to get you to be on the course anyway, so…

Interviewer:	How did you find the transition from education to work then? Was it easy or difficult?

Subject:	At first I found it quite tiring having to be in one place and work for that long a time and it’s probably because they were new people and there were a lot of other things to get to grips with as well. But now, to be honest, I’m finding it easier than my course, because you can – like once you’ve finished you can go home and not worry about it and that’s not something that I’ve had before, and you’ve got evenings and weekends free, which is really nice. I’m almost dreading going back next year because the workload is just so much more.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll help in terms of like you’re working away nine til five, or is your course quite like that anyway?

Subject:	Um, well, I think next year especially on my course is – a lot of the time is the time put in yourself work and it’s structured and I think, from what I’ve heard from friends who are actually doing their final year now, the people who have done placements tend to be a lot more organised and I’ve really found that just getting up early I can get a lot more done during the day, whereas before you – I’d probably put off work and end up doing it in the evening. So it has shown me how constructive you can be if you just use your day properly. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you feel like you’ve had to face any new experience, like office politics or dealing with different types of people?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s – yes, all of the above. Um, there are more boring aspects of work which, you know, filling out timesheets and things like that that everybody has to do which you don’t really think about when you’re learning about the different aspects of design, and there’s also some very difficult people which – I mean luckily most of them I’ve had warnings about, so I’ve been told or suggested how to deal with them, especially because when you’re designing you have certain ways of communicating with other people. Say, if you’re talking to another designer, you’ll just sketch down an idea, but normally you’re communicating with sales people who haven’t got any design background or any mechanical background and you’ve got to explain things in a completely different way and sell your ideas in a different way, which can – it just takes getting used to, just the way you speak to different people, and some people need – you need to go through things thoroughly, whereas other people know what you’re talking about almost straight away, which is – yeah, it’s different coming from somewhere where everybody’s basically thinking along the same lines.

Interviewer:	Do you think that experience will help you when you’re looking for a job in the future?

Subject:	I hope so. I think it will probably help in any job. I think that’s something that you would get from any job.

Interviewer:	Okay, how would you say now then that work and university differ? What are the main differences between the two?

Subject:	Um, I think that university, the work, even if it’s not harder it feels like it just because it’s all on your own back and you’re entirely responsible for it, whereas at work there’s a whole team of people and – I mean if something goes wrong it’s probably not going to affect the rest of your life, whereas it might do here. Um, they seem to be more relaxed at work as well and there isn’t as much pressure and you don’t need to worry about how good you are because, I mean the fact that they’ve already employed you thinks you’re good enough, so it’s not as competitive.

Interviewer:	Okay, do they feel quite supportive where you’re working?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Good. Can you tell me a bit about what your job involves?

Subject:	Yes. I’m on the Design Development team, which isn’t as creative as a lot of the stuff that I’ve done at uni, it’s more to do with – it’s more problem solving of designs rather than just coming up with completely new ideas, even though you do that now and again, and there’s basic stuff which is just lots of vacuum forming to go on shelves, which is what holds all the products, and you also get bigger jobs where, say, you design a whole unit and how everything fits together, which is woodwork and metalwork and… I’ve learnt a lot and the good thing about where I'm working is that there’s also a factory right next to us, so we have to go into the factory and make sure that everything’s being made properly, and I’ve learnt things that I just wouldn’t – they’re just so difficult to get across at university like in the lecture theatre. When you actually see something made and you see all the problems things cause then you understand all the processes much better.

Interviewer:	So it makes sense when you see it for real, rather than just hearing about all the theory?

Subject:	A lot of things have clicked, which has been nice, but yeah, my job’s – they’ve been trying to keep it quite varied and they’ve given me some exciting projects like new designs, the whole unit launches and I’ve got some whole units out in Finland now, which is quite exciting and, um, yeah, it’s also quite nice because you get to see your things being made. Seeing all my designs in production, which not everyone gets to experience really.

Interviewer:	That’s cool. Is the job that you’re doing what you expected you would be doing before you started, or did you know what you would be doing?

Subject:	I don’t know. I – they made it sound like you needed to be a lot better at CAD, but when I got there I found that it was a different package and I just found it so easy to use, so I don’t feel as though it’s – as focused on that as I originally did.

Interviewer:	Do you have to use a lot of CAD at uni?

Subject:	We’re encouraged to, but we don’t have – we don’t really have enough lectures on it. You know, it’s a very difficult package, like it’s renowned for being difficult to use even in industry. I don’t know why they teach it, but yeah – so I was almost dreading that aspect and now I don’t even notice it, and it’s not – there’s not as much sketching work, but I suppose that just depends on me. I probably could introduce that if I wanted to.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility then? 

Subject:	Yeah. At first I was just given smaller jobs and the person who I sit next to oversaw everything that I did and then I was just given jobs on my own and expected to ask questions, and now I’ve been given like equivalent work to the rest of the people in my team to deal with on my own, so I mean I'm already doing exactly the same work as everyone else on the team now, which I'm really pleased about.

Interviewer:	Yeah, cool. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women? Do they employ many women?

Subject:	There aren’t… In other departments it’s almost half/half, almost 60/40 say, men to women. In Design, well in Design Development I think I was the only female in cosmetics and now we’ve got one more, and then in the whole design team there’s about five or six out of about 45.

Interviewer:	That’s interesting as well when they’re the target audience.

Subject:	Yeah, that’s what I said in my interview, it might help me get the job, because I was quite shocked, I really expected there to be more women, because they’re aiming their products at women and they’re selling to women and I’ve spoken to like the other new female designer and she was – we’ve both picked up on some things that we thought were a bit strange. Like they – they’ve thought things would appeal to women and we’ve thought no, or we’ve mentioned things about ‘Oh you wouldn’t want to, you know, put mascaras at the bottom of the unit’ or something like that and the men just wouldn’t really understand why because they don’t actually use the product.

Interviewer:	Do you think the area that you’re working in, it has helped being a woman in terms of doing the work?

Subject:	I think – I think so. Not all the time. Most of the time everybody can do the job, but I have had people approach me asking questions because I'm probably the audience they feel for the products, so they found that quite interesting.

Interviewer:	That is quite interesting. Do the company have a structure or programme in place for you to follow as like a placement student? Do you have targets that you have to achieve or anything like that?

Subject:	Not that I know of. I mean I think they aim for at the end of the placement for me to have covered all the different aspects of what they do, so to have designed a vacuum formed product and an injection moulded product, which is much more expensive, to have worked on a whole unit and to have had a few different opportunities. But I think it – I’ve been told it really depends on the individual and the progress they make and how confident they are to carry out the different jobs.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with how that’s going then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	How do you summarise the experience so far?

Subject:	So far, well I’ve learnt a lot about working just in an office in a kind of – well the way to act and different ways to deal with situations and people and deadlines. Um, I’ve learnt some new skills, computer skills. I’ve learnt knowledge about manufacture, but I’ve also – I’ve also learnt things that I enjoy and I don’t enjoy, like – that I might not have picked up on at university, like liaising with people and sorting out problems that crop up, I really enjoy that and going round and speaking to lots of different people. And I’ve also found that I do enjoy having lots of different projects on because otherwise I do get bored when I’ve only got one thing to do. So yeah, I’ve also – I’ve – it’s not a job that I’d want to do for years and years like some of the people there have been doing, but even bad things like that – that’s probably a negative comment, but it’s still a good thing to learn now, I think. 

Interviewer:	We’ll come back to that later. At the moment what would you say are the benefits of the placement?

Subject:	Benefits, the money is probably the main one.

Interviewer:	Would you recommend someone else to do a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	And would you recommend them to do it at your company?

Subject:	I think the good thing about being in a big company is just… I think it kind of feels more structured and you feel like you’re going to be treated equally.

Interviewer:	Equally in terms of other members of staff?

Subject:	Yeah. You’re given a good amount of responsibility because in a way they don’t rely on each individual quite as much, whereas in a small company if you mess it up it could be really bad for them. So yeah, it’s a good company to work for.

Interviewer:	Would you work for them when you finish if they offered you a job?

Subject:	I think I probably would, but not for more than a year or two. I think I probably would just to – to keep, well, to have a job in the first place, because I think it’s quite difficult to just get a job straight after uni anyway and also I think I could still learn more things but I would – I would run out soon, because it would get repetitive after a while.

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

Subject:	I'm out of practice at drawing. There’s some things that I feel like I need to practice before I come back, which I’m going to definitely have to do.

Interviewer:	Do you have some time off before your back at uni?

Subject:	I do. I’ve got about a month off, which is – which is lucky, but it has been a nice breather and a nice break, you know, and a chance to like sit back and think about how I’m going to do my final year as well.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll use what you’re doing now for your final year project?

Subject:	Probably not, because I want… I want to – at the end of the final year I want to have quite a wide portfolio, so I want to show as many different things I can do as possible. So this year is a whole year’s worth of doing a certain type of, a certain type of design and product, so I want to do something different next year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

Subject:	Hopefully, I'm growing more confident I think in, um, putting across my own ideas and sticking by my ideas and what I’m saying in general. I’ve been told my confidence has grown.

Interviewer:	I was going to say I thought you seem more confident since the last time as well.

Subject:	Really? Um… Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are there any other students on placements?

Subject:	Yes, there’s two guys from my course downstairs and they work in [subsection of company], so not entirely sure what they’ve been doing

Interviewer:	Don’t you see them much then?

Subject:	I don’t work with them, but I do hang around with them, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’re all treated equally, or is that hard to tell because you’re in different areas?

Subject:	Um, I don’t actually. It’s hard to tell. Work-wise I think I’m slightly ahead because I’ve been given more responsibility on certain things sooner. That could be because upstairs it’s a bit more quiet the environment because they’ve got all the bosses up there, so I probably appear like I’m working harder anyway, but I think also – I think I do come across as quite a hard worker, I'm quite studious and organised, which has probably worked to my benefit there. And also, one of the guys downstairs has – he’s just tried too hard to be nice and ends up making all the tea and things like that, whereas I don’t do tea. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think then that it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other students there?

Subject:	Um, I don’t think it’s… 

Interviewer:	Not necessarily in terms of actually doing the work, but maybe in terms of supporting each other?

Subject:	It’s quite nice to be able to ask them questions and to kind of have somebody on your side, because you know they’d stick by you above the organisation or whatever.

Interviewer:	And its quite scary going somewhere new and being the new person.

Subject:	Yeah, it is quite nice to have a few familiar faces right from the start and also, I mean if I have been worried about the work I would have had something – somebody to measure it against, because I think some – I heard, er, I think it was [company], one of the girls was just been given awful jobs to do, but the other people weren’t, so she could already tell that she wasn’t being treated fairly, whereas if there weren’t other students people could just, you know, fob you off and tell you that’s what you’re supposed to do. 

Interviewer:	Okay, has your work involved much team work?

Subject:	There’s – I think there’s seven people in our team. Sometimes you all get together, but usually it’s just - it’s almost working in pairs and then the manager. So a lot of the time I do work with the person who I sit next to, which is nice because you get other opinions straight away, and I’ve had another – another project before Christmas which was quite nice. There were four of us who were working on it and we went down to [town] to get some inspiration and took photos and things, and it is just quite nice to have other people to work with, um, even if – even if I am working on my own, because we’re in a team we can always just go and ask other members, which obviously at the beginning I did quite a lot, asking other people.

Interviewer:	How do you feel about doing team work at work as opposed to team work at uni?

Subject:	Um, I haven’t had anything – any bad experiences like I have at uni. At university it’s a bit more personal because it’s your own grades that are affected and so you do stress a lot more and you feel a lot more responsible for other people’s work and your own, and it’s – I think you feel a lot angrier at people when they don’t put their own effort in. I think at work you’d still feel annoyed when people don’t put the effort in, but you can get away with just doing your exact amount and no more, if you know what I mean.

Interviewer:	Do you think that when you’re at work you have clearer roles within your team?

Subject:	Yeah, I think you have clearer roles and a clearer amount of work to do each, whereas at uni they just kind of leave you to sort it out amongst yourselves, which can end up being unfair and more difficult.

Interviewer:	Do you still think that it helps doing group work at university?

Subject:	In theory, I suppose. I suppose it does.

Interviewer:	Or do you think that you did gain skills out of it that has helped you now?

Subject:	Well, in my last lot of group work on my course I did have to deal with somebody very difficult, which I suppose has helped me; one who didn’t want to do the work. I mean I do kind of get that work still now, because there are certain people who think oh it’s a student, I’ll get them to do part of my work as well because they don’t really know, but now that I’ve kind of cottoned on to it I’ve had to go and find ways of saying ‘No, I’m not going to do that for you’, which is the same thing as doing group work here I suppose.

Interviewer:	Was it easy or difficult telling people?

Subject:	Um, easy, just because I can… I can just say, ‘I’m a student, I don’t really know how to do that, you’ll have to do it for me’ and get out of things like that, although I suppose I wouldn’t be able to do that in industry really, but…

Interviewer:	Has there been particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	Um, there’s only been a couple of people who I’ve disliked working with and that’s just been because – well one of them just keeps on nagging me and coming back and coming back when they don’t need to. In fact, the other one does that as well. Um…

Interviewer:	Like in terms of checking up on you or…?

Subject:	No, in terms of checking up on small details that they have forgotten about and I’ve already told them. Some people have – people in my team I do enjoy working with and I’m quite pleased about, some of them, because they are really helpful and you can just go up to them and ask them a question and even if you ask it ten times they won’t mind and they don’t mind explaining things. The guy who sits next to me, he’s kind – well, I guess he was kind of my supervisor at the beginning, he was – he’s a bit strange, as in he’s quite quiet and a bit difficult to suss out, but over time I’ve quite enjoyed working with him because he is quite honest about – about where I am and what I'm doing and he’s given me – it helps me to kind of gauge how I’m progressing.

Interviewer:	Okay, have you been given a mentor at all?

Subject:	I suppose it’s kind of the person who sits next to me, if anyone.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone else that you could go to for advice at all?

Subject:	Um, there’s two people on my team. One of them has been there for quite a few years and he’s very confident and, you know, knows exactly what he’s doing, and the other one just – he joined about three months before I did and he’s a graduate from my course, so he’s someone who’s more my age and so I can talk to him more as a friend.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone that you would regard as a role model?

Subject:	At work?

Interviewer:	Yeah, or characteristics about different people at work?

Subject:	That’s difficult. Um, people in the creative team, they’ve got some – they’re really good at coming up with ideas and presenting them and then there’s some people in my team who are just… I don’t know, everybody – everyone all combined has got different skills that I would quite like to have or work towards.

Interviewer:	That’s okay. Has anyone from uni been to visit you, like a placement tutor or anything?

Subject:	Yes. He has visited once and I spoke to him today at lunch time because he’s just about to visit me again. And then –

Interviewer:	Did you know him already?

Subject:	Yes, one of my tutors from last year, and, er, the funny thing is that most people where I work, just because it’s in [town], almost everyone did our course at [university] at some point and he was – because he’s been here for 20-odd years or something he just walked in the office and knew everybody. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you think it was useful him coming to visit you? Did he explain why he was visiting?

Subject:	No, not really. He just came to ask us what we’ve been doing so far and then we chatted for a while about completely irrelevant stuff and then he went.

Interviewer:	Did he talk to your manager as well?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Okay. If you had any problems or anything would you be happy to go to that person?

Subject:	Probably, yeah, or at least somebody else in the department. It’s quite helpful me being in [town] anyway because I'm nearby.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Okay, if you did have any problems, do you know whether the university or [company] have got a complaints procedure to follow or anything?

Subject:	I don’t think [company] do, not that I know of, not that I’ve been told about, but there could possibly be one for the university. I expect that if I did complain because it was a placement that they helped me to find as well that they would actually do something about it. I would expect someone to, you know, come and speak to the people at the office or ring up, but at work I think now I know enough people that if I did want to put forward a complaint then somebody would point me in the right direction, yeah.

Interviewer:	You would try and sort it out at work first?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are there appropriate facilities for women in your organisation? Well, it probably won’t affect you working in an office so much, but things like women’s toilets, I don’t know whether you have to wear like safety clothing when you go into the factory and stuff like that?

Subject:	No, luckily. Er, yeah, I think they’ve got everything.

Interviewer:	When you think about your placement do you feel like you’re gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people? 

Subject:	Er, I do get asked things like, because we actually build up prototypes and stuff like that I do get asked, ‘Oh, do you mind doing this?’ or ‘Would you like to help build something’ or ‘Do you mind carrying this, is it too heavy for you?’ whereas I was told, you know, if you’re a guy then you’d just be asked to do it, but I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing and I’m not that strong, to be honest. But I don’t think anyone’s been really surprised or anything. I do – I get doors opened for me, but, you know, just little things like that, which can be annoying at times, because I think well why – why have you bothered waiting, I could have walked anyway, or, you know, you’re in front, you might as well, there’s no space to move around. I think that’s just one little thing that just annoys me anyway.

Interviewer:	You don’t get any jokes or anything?

Subject:	Not that often but I don’t – don’t know. I think jokes like that you kind of… I think any jokes that have been made at me have been because it’s me, as in for each person. Does that make sense?

Interviewer:	I think I know what you mean.

Subject:	As in if you make a joke at a person it’s because of the person not because of the joke you’re making, kind of.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all from doing the placement, because you were talking earlier about there’s things that you’ve realised you do like doing and some things you don’t like doing.

Subject:	Yeah, I think it – it has shown me the pros and cons of the things on my course and my job at the moment and it’s highlighted certain things I enjoy and certain things I don’t enjoy and I’ve also seen – I mean there are some people who have been there for years who love it, but there’s also some people who have been there for years and really want to stop and they don’t like their job any more. That’s motivated me not to be like that. I don’t want – I don’t want to be in a job and complain about it and not doing anything about it. You know, be bored at work and not try and change it. I think it’s probably made me more ambitious than I was before and it’s also reminded me that I really need to – I need to work hard next year, but I also need to make sure that I get the jobs that I enjoy because otherwise eight – well, nine to five is such a long time to work if you’re not enjoying it.

Interviewer:	When you were talking about group work and people that you didn’t like working with, cos’ of how they acted – do you think that’s to do with being a woman or do you think that’s just how those people are with everyone?

Subject:	Um, the guy in particular at university, it was him in a group of three girls and I think girls always seem to be thought of as more organised and they will do the work if you don’t do it, because they need – you know, they want to do well. Um, at work, the people who I’ve found it difficult to work with, it’s only a couple of people and I think they’re quite well known amongst everybody, they’re just – it’s just the way they are, it’s not – they don’t treat people, you know, they’re not treating me differently, it’s just this is how they are with everybody.

Interviewer:	Just awkward? Okay, these are the last few questions now, but they’re questions that I asked you in the last interview. It’s not a test to see if you get the same answer, but to see if your opinions have changed. The hardest one first. What five words would you now use to describe the design and technology industry and the characteristics of it?

Subject:	Um… I think there’s problem-solving even though it’s two words just because such a large amount of design seems to be solving problems to make, you know, to make a better design there’s got to be a problem in the first place. Um…

Interviewer:	I can tell you that you said competitive and exciting last time.

Subject:	I was thinking exciting. I still think exciting.

Interviewer:	That’s good.

Subject:	My opinion is it’s still much more exciting than so many other jobs. Variable, varing, is that a word?

Interviewer:	Lots of variety.

Subject:	Yeah, lots of variety. There’s, you know, there’s so many different aspects to it so… Um…

Interviewer:	Do you still think that it is competitive? I think that you said at the start that it doesn’t seem as competitive as at university?

Subject:	Yeah, I don’t think it is as competitive at work. I just think that like once you’re already there people just consider your design ideas equal to other people’s and even in aspects where you’re not as good at presenting your work, say if someone’s better at, you know, doing sketches, they’ll still consider your proposal just as much, because it’s the ideas they’re after, whereas at university sometimes I think, you know, just if you can make it look pretty it can be considered as a much better design automatically, even if it’s, you know, just a box.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because work is more team-orientated whereas even when you do it in team work at university you’re still working for an individual goal really.

Subject:	Yeah, probably, that’s probably got quite a lot to do with it, because it – yeah, because at work you’re all working towards the same goal, you’re all trying to get one thing. At university you’re all trying to get one thing for yourself. I think that’s the difference.

Interviewer:	Do you think now that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male-dominated environment?

Subject:	Um… I think… I think it’s an advantage when people do treat you differently in the way that I think a lot of men tend to be nicer to women in – just in general or, you know, speak more nicely and not swear as much or joke around as much and get to the point quicker and I – I think I prefer being spoken to like that anyway. Um, I think sometimes you are considered to be a bit more feeble though and maybe not as confident or strong, but I think sometimes that’s my personality anyway as well as being female, where, you know, somebody else might be considered above you, but I think in general it’s a positive difference.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology or engineering?

Subject:	I don’t see why not. I don’t – now that I’m actually working in the industry it’s really not as, you know, it’s not as bad as they make out and even though there’s a very small proportion of women to men, I don’t think there’s a huge difference in the way they’re treated. Having said that, it was pointed out to me today that all the bosses at work are men, which I would have expected in a design team just because, you know, it’s more likely with there being more men than women, but maybe they’ve just got to higher roles just because there are not, you know, a few years ago there were hardly any sort of female designers at all, so it would be impossible for them to work their way up.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think it matters that there aren’t many women in design?

Subject:	Um, not – probably not as much as I did before. I don’t’ think it necessarily affects the outcome, which is what the whole point is anyway, you know, getting good designs, but it is male-dominated, which is probably unfair if it’s putting off people – if it’s putting women off doing it in the first place, if that’s what they want to be.

Interviewer:	Do you think that in the future there will be more women in engineering?

Subject:	Um, yes, but in the near future I don’t think there’s going to be a huge – huge change.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will happen more slowly then?

Subject:	I think – I think there’s going to be – I think it’s going to be male-dominated or, you know, a lot more men for quite a while still, but I think the attitude against women has probably gone now, so…

Interviewer:	Do you think the biggest issue now then is changing people’s attitudes outside the industry?

Subject:	I think it will be –

Interviewer:	Or the perception of what design is?

Subject:	Yeah, and I think it’s probably going back to, you know, just when you’re in school, because before you even get to university there’s hardly any women doing those subjects. So it’s, you know, it’s too late for them to even get into it. That’s probably where it starts.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s everything, thank you very much.

Subject:	You’re welcome.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve just got questions this time about how the placement’s going and what you’re doing and how you think it relates to your course and things like that. So, did you say you started in August?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: August the 31st, so –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Been here quite a while now.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just over six months, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, can you tell me a bit about the organisation that you’re working for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s called [company] and they design and manufacture all the – or a lot of the make displays they’ve got out in the shops at the moment, so all [company] stands and things like that. They also do all of the cigarette stands but that’s a different site. I'm mainly working on cosmetics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that sounds interesting. How useful do you think that your course has been so far to the work that you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it’s a bit difficult. Some – some aspects of my course have been really helpful, but a lot of it is just learning how to use the packages and learning the way of work, which maybe I could have done without doing any of my degree at all really. I might have been slower though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, what about the less technical parts of your degree, like communication skills and things like that? Do you think anything like that has helped?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think all the presentations we’ve done and just generally communicating an idea through drawing has been very helpful and it’s used all the time, and also the fact that on my course, because there are so many different modules, you’ve always got lots of different things going on, whereas on other courses it’s just, say, one essay to concentrate on and in my job I usually have quite a few different things going on, so I probably find it easier to keep my – to get my head around everything and remember everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’ve got good time management skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, is there anything in particular that you wish you had learnt before you started your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, not really. I mean maybe learning extra computer packages would have been helpful, but I think that whichever job you go into you can’t prepare for everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so maybe computers and different packages. (Yeah) Okay, do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for the placement then? (Um) Or is it the same problem again with people doing so many different things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think it – I don’t think there really has been a problem with my placement. I don’t think I was under-prepared for it. I think in the job, like the main aspect they are looking for somebody who’s enthusiastic and who’s hard-working and organised, which they try to get you to be on the course anyway, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you find the transition from education to work then? Was it easy or difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At first I found it quite tiring having to be in one place and work for that long a time and it’s probably because they were new people and there were a lot of other things to get to grips with as well. But now, to be honest, I’m finding it easier than my course, because you can – like once you’ve finished you can go home and not worry about it and that’s not something that I’ve had before, and you’ve got evenings and weekends free, which is really nice. I’m almost dreading going back next year because the workload is just so much more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll help in terms of like you’re working away nine til five, or is your course quite like that anyway?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, well, I think next year especially on my course is – a lot of the time is the time put in yourself work and it’s structured and I think, from what I’ve heard from friends who are actually doing their final year now, the people who have done placements tend to be a lot more organised and I’ve really found that just getting up early I can get a lot more done during the day, whereas before you – I’d probably put off work and end up doing it in the evening. So it has shown me how constructive you can be if you just use your day properly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you feel like you’ve had to face any new experience, like office politics or dealing with different types of people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there’s – yes, all of the above. Um, there are more boring aspects of work which, you know, filling out timesheets and things like that that everybody has to do which you don’t really think about when you’re learning about the different aspects of design, and there’s also some very difficult people which – I mean luckily most of them I’ve had warnings about, so I’ve been told or suggested how to deal with them, especially because when you’re designing you have certain ways of communicating with other people. Say, if you’re talking to another designer, you’ll just sketch down an idea, but normally you’re communicating with sales people who haven’t got any design background or any mechanical background and you’ve got to explain things in a completely different way and sell your ideas in a different way, which can – it just takes getting used to, just the way you speak to different people, and some people need – you need to go through things thoroughly, whereas other people know what you’re talking about almost straight away, which is – yeah, it’s different coming from somewhere where everybody’s basically thinking along the same lines.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that experience will help you when you’re looking for a job in the future?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so. I think it will probably help in any job. I think that’s something that you would get from any job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, how would you say now then that work and university differ? What are the main differences between the two?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think that university, the work, even if it’s not harder it feels like it just because it’s all on your own back and you’re entirely responsible for it, whereas at work there’s a whole team of people and – I mean if something goes wrong it’s probably not going to affect the rest of your life, whereas it might do here. Um, they seem to be more relaxed at work as well and there isn’t as much pressure and you don’t need to worry about how good you are because, I mean the fact that they’ve already employed you thinks you’re good enough, so it’s not as competitive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do they feel quite supportive where you’re working?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Can you tell me a bit about what your job involves?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I’m on the Design Development team, which isn’t as creative as a lot of the stuff that I’ve done at uni, it’s more to do with – it’s more problem solving of designs rather than just coming up with completely new ideas, even though you do that now and again, and there’s basic stuff which is just lots of vacuum forming to go on shelves, which is what holds all the products, and you also get bigger jobs where, say, you design a whole unit and how everything fits together, which is woodwork and metalwork and… I’ve learnt a lot and the good thing about where I'm working is that there’s also a factory right next to us, so we have to go into the factory and make sure that everything’s being made properly, and I’ve learnt things that I just wouldn’t – they’re just so difficult to get across at university like in the lecture theatre. When you actually see something made and you see all the problems things cause then you understand all the processes much better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it makes sense when you see it for real, rather than just hearing about all the theory?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A lot of things have clicked, which has been nice, but yeah, my job’s – they’ve been trying to keep it quite varied and they’ve given me some exciting projects like new designs, the whole unit launches and I’ve got some whole units out in Finland now, which is quite exciting and, um, yeah, it’s also quite nice because you get to see your things being made. Seeing all my designs in production, which not everyone gets to experience really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s cool. Is the job that you’re doing what you expected you would be doing before you started, or did you know what you would be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I – they made it sound like you needed to be a lot better at CAD, but when I got there I found that it was a different package and I just found it so easy to use, so I don’t feel as though it’s – as focused on that as I originally did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to use a lot of CAD at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We’re encouraged to, but we don’t have – we don’t really have enough lectures on it. You know, it’s a very difficult package, like it’s renowned for being difficult to use even in industry. I don’t know why they teach it, but yeah – so I was almost dreading that aspect and now I don’t even notice it, and it’s not – there’s not as much sketching work, but I suppose that just depends on me. I probably could introduce that if I wanted to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. At first I was just given smaller jobs and the person who I sit next to oversaw everything that I did and then I was just given jobs on my own and expected to ask questions, and now I’ve been given like equivalent work to the rest of the people in my team to deal with on my own, so I mean I'm already doing exactly the same work as everyone else on the team now, which I'm really pleased about.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, cool. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women? Do they employ many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There aren’t… In other departments it’s almost half/half, almost 60/40 say, men to women. In Design, well in Design Development I think I was the only female in cosmetics and now we’ve got one more, and then in the whole design team there’s about five or six out of about 45.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s interesting as well when they’re the target audience.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, that’s what I said in my interview, it might help me get the job, because I was quite shocked, I really expected there to be more women, because they’re aiming their products at women and they’re selling to women and I’ve spoken to like the other new female designer and she was – we’ve both picked up on some things that we thought were a bit strange. Like they – they’ve thought things would appeal to women and we’ve thought no, or we’ve mentioned things about ‘Oh you wouldn’t want to, you know, put mascaras at the bottom of the unit’ or something like that and the men just wouldn’t really understand why because they don’t actually use the product.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the area that you’re working in, it has helped being a woman in terms of doing the work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think so. Not all the time. Most of the time everybody can do the job, but I have had people approach me asking questions because I'm probably the audience they feel for the products, so they found that quite interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That is quite interesting. Do the company have a structure or programme in place for you to follow as like a placement student? Do you have targets that you have to achieve or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not that I know of. I mean I think they aim for at the end of the placement for me to have covered all the different aspects of what they do, so to have designed a vacuum formed product and an injection moulded product, which is much more expensive, to have worked on a whole unit and to have had a few different opportunities. But I think it – I’ve been told it really depends on the individual and the progress they make and how confident they are to carry out the different jobs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with how that’s going then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you summarise the experience so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So far, well I’ve learnt a lot about working just in an office in a kind of – well the way to act and different ways to deal with situations and people and deadlines. Um, I’ve learnt some new skills, computer skills. I’ve learnt knowledge about manufacture, but I’ve also – I’ve also learnt things that I enjoy and I don’t enjoy, like – that I might not have picked up on at university, like liaising with people and sorting out problems that crop up, I really enjoy that and going round and speaking to lots of different people. And I’ve also found that I do enjoy having lots of different projects on because otherwise I do get bored when I’ve only got one thing to do. So yeah, I’ve also – I’ve – it’s not a job that I’d want to do for years and years like some of the people there have been doing, but even bad things like that – that’s probably a negative comment, but it’s still a good thing to learn now, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: We’ll come back to that later. At the moment what would you say are the benefits of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Benefits, the money is probably the main one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend someone else to do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And would you recommend them to do it at your company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the good thing about being in a big company is just… I think it kind of feels more structured and you feel like you’re going to be treated equally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Equally in terms of other members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. You’re given a good amount of responsibility because in a way they don’t rely on each individual quite as much, whereas in a small company if you mess it up it could be really bad for them. So yeah, it’s a good company to work for.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work for them when you finish if they offered you a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I probably would, but not for more than a year or two. I think I probably would just to – to keep, well, to have a job in the first place, because I think it’s quite difficult to just get a job straight after uni anyway and also I think I could still learn more things but I would – I would run out soon, because it would get repetitive after a while.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm out of practice at drawing. There’s some things that I feel like I need to practice before I come back, which I’m going to definitely have to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have some time off before your back at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do. I’ve got about a month off, which is – which is lucky, but it has been a nice breather and a nice break, you know, and a chance to like sit back and think about how I’m going to do my final year as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll use what you’re doing now for your final year project?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not, because I want… I want to – at the end of the final year I want to have quite a wide portfolio, so I want to show as many different things I can do as possible. So this year is a whole year’s worth of doing a certain type of, a certain type of design and product, so I want to do something different next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, I'm growing more confident I think in, um, putting across my own ideas and sticking by my ideas and what I’m saying in general. I’ve been told my confidence has grown.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I was going to say I thought you seem more confident since the last time as well.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really? Um… Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there any other students on placements?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, there’s two guys from my course downstairs and they work in [subsection of company], so not entirely sure what they’ve been doing

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Don’t you see them much then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t work with them, but I do hang around with them, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’re all treated equally, or is that hard to tell because you’re in different areas?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t actually. It’s hard to tell. Work-wise I think I’m slightly ahead because I’ve been given more responsibility on certain things sooner. That could be because upstairs it’s a bit more quiet the environment because they’ve got all the bosses up there, so I probably appear like I’m working harder anyway, but I think also – I think I do come across as quite a hard worker, I'm quite studious and organised, which has probably worked to my benefit there. And also, one of the guys downstairs has – he’s just tried too hard to be nice and ends up making all the tea and things like that, whereas I don’t do tea. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think then that it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other students there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t think it’s…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not necessarily in terms of actually doing the work, but maybe in terms of supporting each other?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s quite nice to be able to ask them questions and to kind of have somebody on your side, because you know they’d stick by you above the organisation or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And its quite scary going somewhere new and being the new person.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it is quite nice to have a few familiar faces right from the start and also, I mean if I have been worried about the work I would have had something – somebody to measure it against, because I think some – I heard, er, I think it was [company], one of the girls was just been given awful jobs to do, but the other people weren’t, so she could already tell that she wasn’t being treated fairly, whereas if there weren’t other students people could just, you know, fob you off and tell you that’s what you’re supposed to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, has your work involved much team work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s – I think there’s seven people in our team. Sometimes you all get together, but usually it’s just - it’s almost working in pairs and then the manager. So a lot of the time I do work with the person who I sit next to, which is nice because you get other opinions straight away, and I’ve had another – another project before Christmas which was quite nice. There were four of us who were working on it and we went down to [town] to get some inspiration and took photos and things, and it is just quite nice to have other people to work with, um, even if – even if I am working on my own, because we’re in a team we can always just go and ask other members, which obviously at the beginning I did quite a lot, asking other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel about doing team work at work as opposed to team work at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I haven’t had anything – any bad experiences like I have at uni. At university it’s a bit more personal because it’s your own grades that are affected and so you do stress a lot more and you feel a lot more responsible for other people’s work and your own, and it’s – I think you feel a lot angrier at people when they don’t put their own effort in. I think at work you’d still feel annoyed when people don’t put the effort in, but you can get away with just doing your exact amount and no more, if you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that when you’re at work you have clearer roles within your team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think you have clearer roles and a clearer amount of work to do each, whereas at uni they just kind of leave you to sort it out amongst yourselves, which can end up being unfair and more difficult.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you still think that it helps doing group work at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In theory, I suppose. I suppose it does.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or do you think that you did gain skills out of it that has helped you now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, in my last lot of group work on my course I did have to deal with somebody very difficult, which I suppose has helped me; one who didn’t want to do the work. I mean I do kind of get that work still now, because there are certain people who think oh it’s a student, I’ll get them to do part of my work as well because they don’t really know, but now that I’ve kind of cottoned on to it I’ve had to go and find ways of saying ‘No, I’m not going to do that for you’, which is the same thing as doing group work here I suppose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it easy or difficult telling people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, easy, just because I can… I can just say, ‘I’m a student, I don’t really know how to do that, you’ll have to do it for me’ and get out of things like that, although I suppose I wouldn’t be able to do that in industry really, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has there been particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, there’s only been a couple of people who I’ve disliked working with and that’s just been because – well one of them just keeps on nagging me and coming back and coming back when they don’t need to. In fact, the other one does that as well. Um…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like in terms of checking up on you or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, in terms of checking up on small details that they have forgotten about and I’ve already told them. Some people have – people in my team I do enjoy working with and I’m quite pleased about, some of them, because they are really helpful and you can just go up to them and ask them a question and even if you ask it ten times they won’t mind and they don’t mind explaining things. The guy who sits next to me, he’s kind – well, I guess he was kind of my supervisor at the beginning, he was – he’s a bit strange, as in he’s quite quiet and a bit difficult to suss out, but over time I’ve quite enjoyed working with him because he is quite honest about – about where I am and what I'm doing and he’s given me – it helps me to kind of gauge how I’m progressing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, have you been given a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose it’s kind of the person who sits next to me, if anyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone else that you could go to for advice at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, there’s two people on my team. One of them has been there for quite a few years and he’s very confident and, you know, knows exactly what he’s doing, and the other one just – he joined about three months before I did and he’s a graduate from my course, so he’s someone who’s more my age and so I can talk to him more as a friend.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone that you would regard as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At work?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, or characteristics about different people at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That’s difficult. Um, people in the creative team, they’ve got some – they’re really good at coming up with ideas and presenting them and then there’s some people in my team who are just… I don’t know, everybody – everyone all combined has got different skills that I would quite like to have or work towards.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s okay. Has anyone from uni been to visit you, like a placement tutor or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. He has visited once and I spoke to him today at lunch time because he’s just about to visit me again. And then –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know him already?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, one of my tutors from last year, and, er, the funny thing is that most people where I work, just because it’s in [town], almost everyone did our course at [university] at some point and he was – because he’s been here for 20-odd years or something he just walked in the office and knew everybody. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you think it was useful him coming to visit you? Did he explain why he was visiting?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. He just came to ask us what we’ve been doing so far and then we chatted for a while about completely irrelevant stuff and then he went.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he talk to your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. If you had any problems or anything would you be happy to go to that person?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably, yeah, or at least somebody else in the department. It’s quite helpful me being in [town] anyway because I'm nearby.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Okay, if you did have any problems, do you know whether the university or [company] have got a complaints procedure to follow or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think [company] do, not that I know of, not that I’ve been told about, but there could possibly be one for the university. I expect that if I did complain because it was a placement that they helped me to find as well that they would actually do something about it. I would expect someone to, you know, come and speak to the people at the office or ring up, but at work I think now I know enough people that if I did want to put forward a complaint then somebody would point me in the right direction, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You would try and sort it out at work first?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there appropriate facilities for women in your organisation? Well, it probably won’t affect you working in an office so much, but things like women’s toilets, I don’t know whether you have to wear like safety clothing when you go into the factory and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, luckily. Er, yeah, I think they’ve got everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you think about your placement do you feel like you’re gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I do get asked things like, because we actually build up prototypes and stuff like that I do get asked, ‘Oh, do you mind doing this?’ or ‘Would you like to help build something’ or ‘Do you mind carrying this, is it too heavy for you?’ whereas I was told, you know, if you’re a guy then you’d just be asked to do it, but I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing and I’m not that strong, to be honest. But I don’t think anyone’s been really surprised or anything. I do – I get doors opened for me, but, you know, just little things like that, which can be annoying at times, because I think well why – why have you bothered waiting, I could have walked anyway, or, you know, you’re in front, you might as well, there’s no space to move around. I think that’s just one little thing that just annoys me anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You don’t get any jokes or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not that often but I don’t – don’t know. I think jokes like that you kind of… I think any jokes that have been made at me have been because it’s me, as in for each person. Does that make sense?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I think I know what you mean.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: As in if you make a joke at a person it’s because of the person not because of the joke you’re making, kind of.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all from doing the placement, because you were talking earlier about there’s things that you’ve realised you do like doing and some things you don’t like doing.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it – it has shown me the pros and cons of the things on my course and my job at the moment and it’s highlighted certain things I enjoy and certain things I don’t enjoy and I’ve also seen – I mean there are some people who have been there for years who love it, but there’s also some people who have been there for years and really want to stop and they don’t like their job any more. That’s motivated me not to be like that. I don’t want – I don’t want to be in a job and complain about it and not doing anything about it. You know, be bored at work and not try and change it. I think it’s probably made me more ambitious than I was before and it’s also reminded me that I really need to – I need to work hard next year, but I also need to make sure that I get the jobs that I enjoy because otherwise eight – well, nine to five is such a long time to work if you’re not enjoying it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you were talking about group work and people that you didn’t like working with, cos’ of how they acted – do you think that’s to do with being a woman or do you think that’s just how those people are with everyone?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the guy in particular at university, it was him in a group of three girls and I think girls always seem to be thought of as more organised and they will do the work if you don’t do it, because they need – you know, they want to do well. Um, at work, the people who I’ve found it difficult to work with, it’s only a couple of people and I think they’re quite well known amongst everybody, they’re just – it’s just the way they are, it’s not – they don’t treat people, you know, they’re not treating me differently, it’s just this is how they are with everybody.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Just awkward? Okay, these are the last few questions now, but they’re questions that I asked you in the last interview. It’s not a test to see if you get the same answer, but to see if your opinions have changed. The hardest one first. What five words would you now use to describe the design and technology industry and the characteristics of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um… I think there’s problem-solving even though it’s two words just because such a large amount of design seems to be solving problems to make, you know, to make a better design there’s got to be a problem in the first place. Um…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I can tell you that you said competitive and exciting last time.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was thinking exciting. I still think exciting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My opinion is it’s still much more exciting than so many other jobs. Variable, varing, is that a word?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Lots of variety.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, lots of variety. There’s, you know, there’s so many different aspects to it so… Um…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you still think that it is competitive? I think that you said at the start that it doesn’t seem as competitive as at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I don’t think it is as competitive at work. I just think that like once you’re already there people just consider your design ideas equal to other people’s and even in aspects where you’re not as good at presenting your work, say if someone’s better at, you know, doing sketches, they’ll still consider your proposal just as much, because it’s the ideas they’re after, whereas at university sometimes I think, you know, just if you can make it look pretty it can be considered as a much better design automatically, even if it’s, you know, just a box.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s because work is more team-orientated whereas even when you do it in team work at university you’re still working for an individual goal really.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, probably, that’s probably got quite a lot to do with it, because it – yeah, because at work you’re all working towards the same goal, you’re all trying to get one thing. At university you’re all trying to get one thing for yourself. I think that’s the difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think now that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male-dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um… I think… I think it’s an advantage when people do treat you differently in the way that I think a lot of men tend to be nicer to women in – just in general or, you know, speak more nicely and not swear as much or joke around as much and get to the point quicker and I – I think I prefer being spoken to like that anyway. Um, I think sometimes you are considered to be a bit more feeble though and maybe not as confident or strong, but I think sometimes that’s my personality anyway as well as being female, where, you know, somebody else might be considered above you, but I think in general it’s a positive difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology or engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t see why not. I don’t – now that I’m actually working in the industry it’s really not as, you know, it’s not as bad as they make out and even though there’s a very small proportion of women to men, I don’t think there’s a huge difference in the way they’re treated. Having said that, it was pointed out to me today that all the bosses at work are men, which I would have expected in a design team just because, you know, it’s more likely with there being more men than women, but maybe they’ve just got to higher roles just because there are not, you know, a few years ago there were hardly any sort of female designers at all, so it would be impossible for them to work their way up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think it matters that there aren’t many women in design?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, not – probably not as much as I did before. I don’t’ think it necessarily affects the outcome, which is what the whole point is anyway, you know, getting good designs, but it is male-dominated, which is probably unfair if it’s putting off people – if it’s putting women off doing it in the first place, if that’s what they want to be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that in the future there will be more women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yes, but in the near future I don’t think there’s going to be a huge – huge change.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will happen more slowly then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think there’s going to be – I think it’s going to be male-dominated or, you know, a lot more men for quite a while still, but I think the attitude against women has probably gone now, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the biggest issue now then is changing people’s attitudes outside the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will be –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or the perception of what design is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and I think it’s probably going back to, you know, just when you’re in school, because before you even get to university there’s hardly any women doing those subjects. So it’s, you know, it’s too late for them to even get into it. That’s probably where it starts.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You’re welcome.
